covers.quote: Remember to avoid blocks of italics wherever possible.

rules.quote:
Don’t use italics for:

- large blocks of text
- material that would normally be in italics but is set apart (such as a list of titles under a heading)
- aggregation pages (such as a page listing legislation/type(principal)/collection(act))).
rules.specification: Do not format large chunks/blocks of text or isolated lists/aggregation pages in italic type.
rules.violation_condition: italics used on large blocks of text, on material set apart such as lists of titles under a heading, or on aggregation pages
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Consolidates prohibitions on chunks and lists of italic text across the page.

rules.quote: Don’t use italics for the titles of sacred texts, such as the Bible or the Koran.
rules.violation_condition: titles of sacred texts (such as the Bible or the Koran) written in italics
rules.why: Explicit prohibition against italicising sacred texts.

covers.quote: Italicise titles of stand-alone works, legal cases and Acts
Unpublished works are in roman type.

examples.note: Emerald city is italicised

parts.quote: David Williamson’s play Emerald city was first performed in 1987.

examples.note: Piano concerto no. 3 is italicised

parts.quote: Elena Kats-Chernin’s Piano concerto no. 3is a recent work by the award-winning composer.

examples.note: Self-portrait, after George Lambert is italicised

parts.quote: In 2018, Yvette Coppersmith won the Archibald Prize with Self-portrait, after George Lambert.

rules.quote:
Use italics for the titles of these published works:

- books and periodicals
- plays
- classics
- most musical compositions
- ballets and operas
- films, videos and podcasts
- blogs
- television and radio programs
- artworks.
rules.violation_condition: titles of published stand-alone works (such as books, plays, periodicals, films, blogs, artworks) written in roman type rather than italics
when: Unpublished works are in roman type.
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Specific list of published works to italicise, noting exception for unpublished works.

covers.quote: Reverse italics in titles of published works

examples.note: Reverse italics used for The Ghan inside an italicised book title

parts.quote: Gone onThe Ghanand other great railway journeys of Australia [The Ghan is the official name of a train; it would normally be italicised.]

rules.quote: In some titles, there are words that would normally be italicised. To make sure they stand out from the rest of the italicised title, write the words in roman type. This is called ‘reverse italics’.
rules.violation_condition: words within an italicised title that would normally be italicised not set in roman type (reverse italics)
rules.why: Clear rule requiring reverse italics inside italicised titles.

examples.note: Case name and Act are in italics; informal title and bill are in roman type

parts.quote: The Franklin Dam Case is the informal title of Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983) 158 CLR 1. The case led to the World Heritage Properties Conservation Bill which became an Act in 1983. In 1999, the Act was replaced by parts of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.

rules.quote: Use italics for primary legislation and legal cases but not for delegated legislation or bills.
rules.violation_condition: primary legislation or legal cases not written in italics, or delegated legislation or bills written in italics
when: Informal and common titles are in roman type.
rules.why: Covers typography for legal cases, Acts, delegated legislation, and bills.

covers.quote: Italics contrast words and phrases that are not in English from surrounding text.
Standard Australian English can absorb words or phrases from other languages. Write these ‘borrowed’ words without italics or accent marks.

examples.note: French phrase set in italics

parts.quote: The more things change, plus c’est la même.

examples.note: Borrowed word 'barista' written in roman type

parts.quote: John was the head barista at the department’s coffee shop.

rules.quote: Set off most foreign words and phrases
rules.specification: Italicise foreign words and phrases unless they are absorbed into standard Australian English.
rules.violation_condition: foreign words and phrases that have no English equivalent not set in italics
when: Borrowed words absorbed into standard Australian English are written in roman type without accent marks.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Rule on italicising foreign words, with exception for absorbed borrowed words.

rules.quote: Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages.
rules.violation_condition: names or words from First Nations languages written in italics
rules.why: Direct, explicit negative rule.

covers.quote: Don’t use italics for Latin shortened forms

examples.note: Abbreviation cf. is in roman type, full Latin word confer is italicised

parts.quote: The abbreviation ‘cf.’ is from the Latin word confer and means ‘compare’.

rules.quote: Write the full Latin word in italics but not the shortened form.
rules.violation_condition: Latin shortened forms written in italics, or full Latin words written in roman type
rules.why: G-4: Rule governing full Latin terms vs Latin abbreviations.

rules.quote: Instead, to draw attention to words with special meaning, use single quotation marks.
rules.specification: Use single quotation marks, not italics, for introducing a technical term or words with special meaning.
rules.violation_condition: italics used instead of single quotation marks to define or introduce a technical term for the first time or draw attention to words with special meaning
rules.why: E-1, G-4: Explicit instruction to avoid italics for technical terms and use single quotation marks instead.

examples.note: Britannia is italicised, the preceding 'the' is roman

parts.quote: Until 1997, Queen Elizabeth II would use the Britannia to sail to official visits overseas. [The definite article ‘the’ is in roman type, while the ship’s official name is in italics.]

examples.note: Vehicle proper name Great Southern Land is italicised

parts.quote: Qantas uses Australian names like Great Southern Land for the Dreamliner fleet.

rules.quote: The name is in italics excluding any definite article. The brand or type of vehicle is in roman type.
rules.violation_condition: proper names of vehicles not written in italics, definite articles before vehicle names written in italics, or vehicle brand/type written in italics
rules.why: G-2: Covers proper names of vehicles and the rule for definite articles/brands.

covers.quote: Write the scientific names of infectious organisms, including some bacteria and fungi, in italics.

examples.note: Acacia phlebocarpa is in italics, tabletop wattle is in roman

parts.quote: Acacia phlebocarpa is the scientific name for the tabletop wattle.

examples.note: Staphylococcus aureus is in italics, golden staph is in roman

parts.quote: Certain strains of the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus cause golden staph.

rules.quote: Use italics for the genus and species, including any subspecies, but not for the common name.
rules.violation_condition: scientific names (genus, species, subspecies) not written in italics, or common names written in italics
rules.why: G-2: Combines genus/species formatting with organism scientific names.

covers.quote: If the italics is part of the original text, write ‘emphasis from original’ in the square brackets following the quotation.

examples.note: Shows [emphasis added] following quote where italics were introduced

parts.quote: ‘Subsequently, in 1903, Parliament passed a unanimous resolution that it should be flown.’ [emphasis added]

rules.quote: If you do this, write ‘emphasis added’ in square brackets following the italicised text.
rules.violation_condition: italics added to a quotation without '[emphasis added]' following the italicised text
when: If italics is part of the original quotation, write '[emphasis from original]' in square brackets following the quotation.
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates handling of emphasis annotations in quotations.
